When I call a candidate after a first round, I relay what the panel said, but I never read it to him verbatim. I tell him the chair said she would want to hear more about cash, or that one director had a reservation about his sector. Then I stop and I listen. The weak candidates get defensive, or they ask me who said it. The strong ones ask a different question. They ask what the panel might want to see in the second round, and whether they could send anything before it. That tells me they have taken the feedback on board, and it is usually the moment I decide to put in a good word with the chief executive.

I have hired four finance directors, and the second interview is the one I run myself. The first thing I ask is what the candidate heard in round one. Most of them gloss over it. The best one I ever hired opened his notebook and said, your chief people officer told me the role would include technology, and the headhunter said you might sell the print business. Is that still on the table? Two of those things were wrong. I corrected them in a minute, and we spent the rest of the hour on the real job. Secondhand information is not a problem. Taking it into the room without checking it is.
